newsitem.title: BRAZIL: More tapes on Brazil vote scandal exist-newspaper.
newsitem.headline: More tapes on Brazil vote scandal exist-newspaper.

text.p: There are more recordings of conversations between Brazilian lawmakers and an unidentified speaker dubbed "Mr X" suggesting the alleged cash-for-votes scandal rocking Congress last week involves more legislators than those linked to the alleged scheme so far, a newspaper reported Sunday citing the unnamed Mr X.

Folha de Sao Paulo daily, citing taped conversations between congressmen and Mr X, alleged last week that five lawmakers took bribes to vote in favor of a bill that would allow President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to stand for a second term next year.

Brazilian financial markets were roiled from last Tuesday to Thursday when Folha for three straight days published its exlusive stories on the alleged vote-buying affair. The articles drew swift denials from the politicians that the daily linked to the scam.

"I still have many tapes with many more people," Mr X told Folha de Sao Paulo in an nterview published Sunday. "I will not reveal them. What has been published is more than enough to prove the rottenness surrounding the re-election bill."

The re-election bill, which would allow the president, state governors and mayors to run for a second consecutive term in office, was approved by the Chamber of Deputies in January in what was seen as the biggest political test for the two-year-old Cardoso administration. The bill is due to be voted on in the Senate.
Cardoso Thursday defended his government as honest, denied any knowledge of the allegations and pledged to punish those found guilty in the matter.

According to the purported conversations published in Folha, five congressmen from Acre were paid $188,679 each by the governors of Acre and Amazonas state so they would vote in favor of the re-election bill.
Both governors and the five congressmen named denied the accusations.

The paper also published details of a purported taped conversation allegedly between one congressman and "Mr X" in which it is suggested Brazil Communications Minister Sergio Motta offered the lawmaker a television concession for his vote on the re-election bill.
Motta denied all allegations of wrongdoing and said the reports were absurd and untruthful.
"The issues which have come up through the declarations are repulsive and must be rigorously investigated and punished if proven," Motta said Thursday.
In the interview published Sunday, Mr X said it was wrong to think that the state of Acre was the cradle of corruption because such irregularities took place throughout Brazil.

The scandal has come at a delicate time for the government which is trying to push through Congress its civil service and pension reforms, as well as laws on the opening of the state oil monopoly and on the privization of the telecommunications sector.
Financial markets plunged on news of the scandal with the Sao Paulo stock exchange falling 3.43 percent Wednesday following reports of Motta's alleged involvement in the vote buying scheme.

A congressional inquiry investigating the matter is due to report its findings this week, but left-wing opposition parties hope to garner enough support to launch a more wide ranging special parliamentary inquiry, known as CPI. They also want the re-election bill to be put on hold.
